title: Handoff-prefetch sweep: misaligned token-window handoff and cross-model throughput-skew analysis
content:
Summary:

This note captures a targeted sweep of prefetch/handoff behavior observed across Llama, Mistral and Qwen family models when operating with long-context requests and MoE routing enabled. We observed a reproducible throughput skew and increased tail latency for MoE workloads in mixed token-window scenarios where client tokenization and the serving runtime's prefetch horizon are not aligned. The goal of the sweep was to 1) identify the micro-root cause of the skew, 2) quantify impact across models and sequence lengths, and 3) propose short/medium-term mitigations that are low-risk to ship.

Why we care:
- Customer SLA sensitivity: Dedicated/Dedicated+Private tenants see variable latency tails for chat long-context use cases.
- Cost: Unplanned throughput drop increases GPU-hours per token for MoE models.
- Predictability: Mixed workloads (non-MoE plus MoE) exacerbate head-of-line and serialization effects.

Experiment snapshot (common config):
- Runtime: rwd-infer/runtime:v5.2-experiments (profiling flags enabled)
- Hardware: A100-80GB (single GPU per worker), PCIe-hosted NVMe for prefix cache, standard NIC
- Models: llama-2-13b-chat (dense), mistral-instruct-7b-v1 (dense), qwen-14b-v1 (dense), qwen-moe-16b-32e (MoE variant used for the core observations)
- Token windows tested: 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192
- Prefetch horizon param (runtime): 96 tokens default, swept {32,64,96,128,256}
- Batch mix: single-request heavy (latency-sensitive) and small-batch multi-request (throughput-sensitive)
- Metrics collected: p50/p90/p99 latency, tokens/sec per-GPU, GPU-occupancy timeline, kernel launch latencies, PCIe DMA bursts, memcpy time, KV-cache hit ratio, gating entropy, routing fanout distribution, RPC handoff durations

Observed phenomena (high level):
1) Misaligned tokenization -> repeated cold expert activation: When the client splits user context into chunks that are offset from the runtime's prefetch window boundary (example: tokenizer chunk boundaries at 768 tokens while prefetch horizon aligned at 96 tokens multiple), the routing/gating layer frequently sees the same expert coldstart on repeated handoffs. That manifests as periodic spikes in memcpy + DMA activity followed by cpu-side serialization and a drop in tokens/sec.
2) Cross-model divergence: Dense models (Llama/Mistral/Qwen dense) show modest throughput degradation (<10%) with larger windows, but MoE model shows 15-40% throughput collapse and 20-60% increase in p99 depending on gating entropy and sequence length.
3) Short-lived fallback storms: For long contexts with token overlap between new requests and cached prefixes, prefetch incorrectly invalidates some KV cache entries (observed via cache-index mismatch logs), causing fallback to slower expert fetch path and subsequent re-population — leading to bursts of synchronous IO.
4) Head-of-line and serialization: Handoff RPCs during the burst periods cause worker thread starvation in the scheduler queue, which increases end-to-end queuing latency for unrelated requests.

Representative numbers (example run, qwen-moe-16b-32e):
- 2048 tokens, prefetch=96 (default): baseline tokens/sec 18k -> observed drop to 12k during misaligned bursts (~33% drop); p99 3.1s -> 4.9s (58% increase)
- 4096 tokens, prefetch=96: tokens/sec baseline 15k -> 9k (~40% drop); p99 3.9s -> 6.2s
- Increasing prefetch to 256 tokens reduced burst frequency but increased steady-state memory pressure and occasional OOM-like eviction events on smaller GPUs.

Key traces and profiling artifacts (high-level):
- trace-id: rwt-20251004-0389 (qwen-moe 2048 tokens): shows repeated memcpy CPU→GPU peaks ~every 96 tokens; gated-expert fanout spikes from 2→8 and back, correlated with decreases in GPU occupancy for ~80ms.
- flamegraph: /artifacts/handshake-flame-qwen-moe-2048.svg (linked in PR)
- kernel-latency-table: kern-delta-20251004.csv (attached to PR)

Root cause analysis (hypothesis consolidated):
- At the handoff boundary between prefix/cached KV and new token region, the runtime currently schedules a prefetch of upcoming token blocks with a fixed horizon. If client-side tokenization produces a chunk alignment that does not fall on the same token-block boundaries, the runtime may end up prefetching blocks that are insufficiently contiguous for the gating layer, triggering cold expert selection repeatedly as the router observes new token patterns at each boundary.
- The cold expert path is IO-heavy: it requires copying expert weights/activations into GPU working set, possibly incurring PCIe DMA, leading to transient reductions in compute throughput while pages/activations are replicated.
- For MoE: gating entropy multiplies the probability of touching different experts across successive handoffs. When combined with misaligned prefetch, we see a combinatorial increase in cache misses and memcpy events.

Why dense models are less affected:
- Dense models don't have expert fanout variability; prefetch misalignment still causes KV-cache miss and memcpy overhead, but the amortized cost is lower and less bursty.

Mitigations (short-to-medium term):
Short (low risk, ship first):
- Prefetch alignment heuristic: at request ingress compute tokenizer-derived chunk offsets (if client sends tokenization boundaries) and align runtime prefetch windows to those offsets when available. Fallback to current behavior otherwise. (Estimated dev effort: 2–3 engineer-days; small API change optional)
- Handshake debounce: add a tiny (~2–4ms) soft-debounce before scheduling heavyweight expert prefetch to allow in-flight tokenization to settle for browser/mobile clients that flush in chunks. (1–2 engineer-days)
- Instrument gating entropy to per-request logs and emit high-cardinality metric to alert on rising entropy. (1 engineer-day)

Medium (higher risk / requires validation):
- Prefetch horizon adaptive controller: increase horizon under stable cache hit regimes and shrink under repeated cache misses; requires A/B validation to avoid memory pressure regressions. (2–3 sprints)
- Asynchronous expert warmup: convert expert weight fetch to non-blocking pre-warm path that doesn't block critical compute threads — needs kernel/driver changes and careful backpressure. (longer-term, 2+ sprints)
- Route-aware packing: co-schedule requests predicted to touch overlapping expert sets to reduce duplicate fetches. Requires gating predictor and scheduler integration. (researchy; medium risk)

Operational mitigations (immediate):
- Alert on sudden PCIe DMA burst frequency and p99 memory-copy time. Add a runbook that scales an extra dedicated-worker pool that disables MoE eager prefetch for tenants experiencing bursts.
- Canary: enable prefetch alignment heuristic for a small percentage of traffic on dedicated clusters to measure real-world impact.

Follow-ups (action items):
- [Aisha] Draft RFC for "prefetch alignment" with API extension for optional client token-boundary hint (ETA: 2025-10-17).
- [Daniel] Implement soft-debounce + gating-entropy metric (ETA: 2025-10-10).
- [Marta] Re-run sweep with networked NVMe (remote cache) vs local NVMe to validate whether storage topology changes burst characteristics (ETA: 2025-10-20).
- [Ray] PoC of async expert warmup (kernel hook) using background CUDA streams and pinned memory pipeline (ETA: 2 weeks).

Open questions and discussion points:
- Should we require client-side token boundary metadata in the public API? Pros: deterministic alignment and lower runtime complexity. Cons: barrier to adoption for many clients.
- Is there an affordable heuristic for aligning prefetch without client hints? (e.g., detect repeating tokenization patterns and shift window adaptively)
- Do different MoE topologies (expert count / fanout) change recommended prefetch horizon? We saw hints that wide-expert setups are more fragile.

Notes on experiment reproducibility:
- All runs encoded random but repeatable seeds; workloads are available under /bench/long-window/handoff-sweep/ with run scripts; use runtime:v5.2-experiments to reproduce observed traces.
- Attached scripts annotate token-boundary offsets in logs for easy correlation.

Appendix (short traces & logs):
- sample log snippet (trace rwt-20251004-0389):
  [2025-10-04T12:03:14.321Z] REQUEST r=0 id=... tokens=2048 chunk_offset=768 prefetch_win=96 -> schedule_prefetch(blocks=[768..864])
  [2025-10-04T12:03:14.402Z] ROUTER r=0 gating_entropy=0.67 fanout=[3] -> experts touched=[12,4,23]
  [2025-10-04T12:03:14.481Z] DMA start host->gpu size=42MB (expert-12 weights)
  [2025-10-04T12:03:14.520Z] THREAD scheduler wait=12ms queue=5
  [2025-10-04T12:03:14.602Z] GPU kernel launch forward_layer_x time=6ms
  [2025-10-04T12:03:14.682Z] CACHE index mismatch: prefix-key=abc123 expected=0x1a found=0x0

Concluding thoughts:
- The misaligned token-window handoff problem is subtle because it is an interaction between client tokenization behavior and server prefetch heuristics, magnified for MoE models by gating variability.
- Low-risk mitigations (alignment heuristic + soft debounce + metrics) should materially reduce burst frequency and are worth shipping quickly while we prototype more robust controller-level solutions.

Please review and flag any missing tests or additional metrics we should capture in the next sweep.
